title: Resolution & Marriage
content_html:
The Lydia Crisis

Lydia’s elopement with Wickham is the novel’s crisis. She runs away from Brighton, believing they will marry. In Regency society, an unmarried woman living with a man was a catastrophic scandal that would ruin her entire family. Mrs Bennet is hysterical. The real question is: who will marry any Bennet sister now that the family name is disgraced?

Wickham has no intention of marrying Lydia — she has no fortune. The elopement exposes his true character as a rake, not the victim he claimed to be. Mr Bennet’s negligence is finally exposed: he retreated into his library while his youngest daughters ran wild. “I am heartily ashamed of myself,” he admits — but the damage is done.

Key Fact

Lydia’s elopement exposes: (1) Wickham’s predatory nature, (2) Mr Bennet’s parental negligence, and (3) the precariousness of women’s reputations in Regency society. One daughter’s scandal threatens all five sisters’ futures.

Darcy’s Secret Intervention

Darcy quietly resolves the crisis. He tracks Wickham and Lydia to London, pays Wickham’s considerable debts, and bribes him to marry Lydia. He does this entirely for Elizabeth’s sake, asking for no recognition. When the Gardiners reveal his role, Elizabeth is astonished: the man she once despised has saved her family at enormous personal cost.

Darcy’s intervention is the novel’s most powerful proof of genuine transformation. He helps the family he once called ‘degrading.’ He pays off the man who tried to seduce his own sister. He asks for nothing in return. This is not pride or obligation — it is selfless love. Austen contrasts Darcy’s actions with Wickham’s: one man sacrifices for love, the other exploits it.

Lady Catherine arrives at Longbourn to demand Elizabeth promise never to accept Darcy. She calls the Bennets “obstinate, headstrong” and asks: “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?” Elizabeth refuses: “I am only resolved to act in that manner, which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you.” This confrontation is Austen’s most direct clash between individual merit and aristocratic entitlement. Elizabeth wins — and Lady Catherine’s report of her defiance ironically encourages Darcy to propose again.

The Second Proposal

Darcy proposes again during a walk near Longbourn. His tone is entirely changed: “an eagerness that had nothing of pride or resentment about it.” He speaks with humility and vulnerability. Elizabeth accepts. Austen deliberately contrasts the two proposals: the first was pride assuming gratitude; the second is genuine love expressed with honest uncertainty.

When Elizabeth tries to explain her changed feelings, she jokes: “I believe I must date it from my first seeing his beautiful grounds at Pemberley.” This is classic Austen — the joke contains truth (Pemberley did influence her) while deflecting from the real, complex process of revised understanding that brought her to this point.

Key Fact

First proposal: pride, ‘degradation,’ expects gratitude, delivered indoors formally. Second proposal: humility, eagerness, no class references, delivered outdoors on a walk. The contrast proves genuine transformation in both characters.

The Resolution

Three marriages resolve the novel: Elizabeth and Darcy (love with mutual respect), Jane and Bingley (gentle love rewarded), and Lydia and Wickham (a cautionary tale of passion without judgement). Mr Bennet is chastened by the Lydia crisis. Mrs Bennet is delighted — for entirely material reasons: “three daughters married! Ten thousand a year!” Her response confirms that she has learned nothing, providing one final comic irony.

Some critics argue the ending is too neat — the heroine gets the richest man, the villain is punished, the good are rewarded. But Austen includes complications that prevent simple satisfaction. Lydia remains unrepentant. Wickham is bought, not reformed. Mrs Bennet learns nothing. Mr Bennet retreats again. The ideal marriage exists alongside continuing foolishness, suggesting that individual happiness is possible but social reform is not.
exam_tip_html: When comparing the two proposals, focus on specific language changes. First proposal: ‘degradation,’ ‘against his will.’ Second: ‘eagerness,’ no class references. This precise AO2 comparison, linked to Darcy’s transformation (AO1) and Regency class expectations (AO3), earns top-band marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Lydia’s elopement tests every character and exposes parental failure and social vulnerability.
  • Darcy’s secret intervention — selfless, uncredited, costly — is the ultimate proof of his transformation.
  • The second proposal contrasts perfectly with the first: humility and vulnerability replace pride and condescension.

glossary_terms.definition: A man who pursues women dishonourably, without moral scruple.
Fundamental character change through self-reflection and moral effort.
When events produce the opposite of what was expected — Lady Catherine’s interference encourages the marriage she opposes.
Public standing, especially important for women in Regency society where scandal could ruin a family.
The final section of narrative where conflicts are resolved.
